Learning Objectives
Review the clinical manifestations of aseptic loosening after total hip arthroplasty.
Evaluate the radiographic findings of aseptic loosening after total hip arthroplasty.
Identify the differential diagnosis for aseptic loosening after total hip arthroplasty.
Determine the surgical treatment options for aseptic loosening after total hip arthroplasty.
Overview
Definition: loss of implant fixation in a previously well-fixed implant without a mechanical or an
infectious etiology1

Epidemiology
Radiographic findings of aseptic loosening may be observed in 25% of prostheses.2
Prior generation cement techniques resulted in a 10% to 15% aseptic loosening revision rate at
15 years after total hip arthroplasty (THA).3
Current generation cement techniques and uncemented porous-coated prostheses result in a
5% aseptic loosening revision rate at 15 years after THA.3
Young (<50 years) patients, male patients, high-activity patients, and patients with obesity have
an increased risk for aseptic loosening after THA.3-6

Epidemiology
Aseptic loosening is a common cause of failure after total joint arthroplasty.7 It is the
predominant form of long-term failure; however, with the invention of ultra-low–
molecular-weight highly cross-linked polyethylene, the incidence has substantially
decreased. Patients who are young or obese or who have high activity levels have an
increased risk for clinically important aseptic THA loosening.
Basic Science and Causes
Osteolysis is the most common cause of aseptic loosening and primarily results from reaction
to wear particles.
The particle that most commonly causes a reaction is polyethylene.
Other causes of osteolysis include metallosis and polymethyl methacrylate particles (ie, bone
cement).
Wear particles can be generated from all junctions in THA (ie, liner-head, head-neck).
The predominant modes of wear in THA are adhesive wear and abrasive wear.8
Release of wear particles stimulates macrophage cytokines and upregulation of the receptor
activator of nuclear factor kappa-B/receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand
pathway.
The net result is an increase in effective joint space.9
Stress shielding is another potential cause.

It results from bone resorption in unloaded bone (ie, proximal femur in a diaphyseal-fitting
stem, stem modulus mismatch in osteoporotic bone).

Basic Science and Causes
Although aseptic loosening has many causes, osteolysis is the most common etiology.
Osteolysis primarily results from polyethylene wear; however, other factors include
metallosis from metal-on-metal interactions and polymethyl methacrylate particles.7,10
The predominant modes of wear in THA implants are adhesive wear and abrasive wear.
Adhesive wear occurs if a harder surface (ie, cobalt-chromium or a ceramic head ball)
interacts with a softer surface (ie, polyethylene) and causes breakdown of the softer
surface. Abrasive wear occurs with the asperities on a hard surface and causes
mechanical breakdown of an articulating softer surface, resulting in particle release.
Regardless of the mode of wear, the release of polyethylene particles causes
macrophage activation. Macrophage activation stimulates the production of tumor
necrosis factor alpha, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6, which promote upregulation of
the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B/receptor activator of nuclear factor
kappa-B ligand pathway.2 Upregulation of this pathway results in a state of bone
catabolism surrounding the implant and increases the effective joint space (Figure 1).
The effective joint space is defined as the interaction of bone with synovial joint fluid. In
well-fixed implants, this interaction is minimal; however, as osteolysis progresses, the
synovial fluid comes in contact with the retro-acetabular space and the distal aspect of
the femoral stem, resulting in prosthetic loosening.

Figure 1 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates the concept of effective joint space. In
normal, well-fixed implants, the effective joint space is defined by the green lines, which
include the hip capsule. This is because of the well-fixed nature of the implant on the
femoral and acetabular sides, which do not allow egress of synovial fluid from the hip
capsule. In patients with a loose femoral implant, the effective joint space is increased to
include the green and red lines. In the left hip implant, loosening of the prosthesis from
the bone allows for egress of fluid from the hip capsule down the femoral shaft around
the prosthesis. Similarly, in patients with a loose acetabular cup, the effective joint space
includes the area surrounding the cup and the screws. (Courtesy of R. Mayur Amin, MD,
Redwood City, CA.)
Stress shielding is another cause of periprosthetic lucency observed on radiographs and
loss of bony implant support. Stress shielding occurs because of Wolff’s law, which states
that bone responds to mechanical load. Therefore, areas undergoing high mechanical

experiencing less force will undergo catabolism. Therefore, bone resorption occurs in
patients in whom the bone does not undergo a mechanical load (ie, proximal femur in a
diaphyseal-fitting stem) after prosthesis implantation11 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 AP radiographs of the right hip of a patient obtained immediately after total hip
arthroplasty with the use of a fully porous-coated, press-fit stem (A) and 10 years
postoperatively (B). Note the presence of a distal spot weld at the location at which the
implant is well fixed and consequent cortical hypertrophy in this area because of the
increased mechanical load. Note the relative decrease in cortical thickness proximal to
the spot weld and lucency indicating lack of mechanical stress, or stress shielding.
Although stress shielding and osteolysis may result in lucency about the implant, the
etiology of the lucency is different. (Reproduced with permission from Rivière C,

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Impending aseptic loosening frequently is clinically silent and, therefore, must be closely
monitored if identified.
Pain is nonspecific but frequently observed in patients with aseptic loosening. Acetabular
component loosening correlates with groin pain, whereas stem loosening typically manifests
as thigh pain.
Start-up pain is a hallmark of a loose THA implant. Start-up pain is defined as pain with the first
several steps of weight bearing and progressive dissipation of pain with implant loading.

Clinical Presentation
Given that many prostheses exhibit incomplete or nonprogressive radiolucency, the
diagnosis of aseptic loosening should be made in combination with a physical
examination. Clinical signs of implant loosening include groin pain (acetabulum), thigh
pain (femoral stem), and start-up pain. The latter is defined as pain on the first several
steps of gait that is reduced after progressive loading (Resource 1).
Radiographic Findings
The most common findings include progression of radiolucent lines or implant subsidence.
Best observed on serial radiographs (Figure 3)
Subsidence can be measured by a change in implant position on the calcar or by a change in
the relationship of the femoral head with respect to the greater trochanter.
Radiolucent lines are defined based on Gruen (femur) and DeLee and Charnley (acetabulum)
zones.12,13

Aseptic loosening is most easily defined by the progression of radiolucent lines or
implant subsidence on serial radiographs.8 Therefore, comparison of new radiographs
with prior radiographs is essential to diagnose aseptic loosening. Radiolucent lines are
described based on thee Gruen zone and the DeLee and Charnley zone (Figure 6).
Implant subsidence may be assessed on serial radiographs by evaluating for changes in
the femoral stem position relative to the calcar or the position at which a horizontal line
from the tip of the trochanter intersects the femoral head. In cemented implants,
fracture of the cement mantle or lucency at the implant-cement interface suggests
prosthetic loosening;1 however, changes at the cement-bone interface may be the result
of normal remodeling.8 Another indication of aseptic loosening is bone formation distal
to the tip of the implant; this is known as a pedestal. In addition, eccentric polyethylene
wear may be a sign of current or impending substantial osteolysis.
Figure 6 AP pelvis radiograph (A) demonstrates the DeLee and Charnley zones of
acetabular loosening, and lateral left hip radiograph (B) demonstrates the Gruen zones
of femoral loosening. (Courtesy of R. Mayur Amin, MD, Redwood City, CA.)
Differential Diagnosis
After the diagnosis of a loose implant is made, the differential diagnosis includes aseptic
versus septic etiology.

Serum (ie, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level) and synovial fluid (ie, cell
count with differential, culture) laboratory studies may be indicated per the Musculoskeletal
Infection Society criteria.
Serum laboratory studies also may be indicated in patients with aseptic etiology (ie, cobalt-
chromium levels to determine metallosis).

Differential Diagnosis
For patients with clinical and radiographic signs of implant loosening, the primary
differential diagnosis includes aseptic versus septic loosening. An appropriate workup to
rule out an infectious etiology may include serum and/or synovial fluid laboratory
studies according to the Musculoskeletal Infection Society criteria. The cause of aseptic
loosening also may be determined via serum laboratory studies (ie, cobalt-chromium
levels to determine metallosis). In patients with severe metallosis, automated synovial
cell counts may be falsely elevated, and a manual cell count should be performed.15
Alternative Diagnostic Tests
Clinical examination and serial radiographs are the primary methods for diagnosing aseptic
loosening.
The role of alternative tests, such as bone scintigraphy, serum laboratory studies, or positron
emission tomography (PET), is limited because these tests cannot reliably diagnose aseptic
loosening.

Alternative Diagnostic Tests
The diagnosis of aseptic loosening relies on physical examination in combination with
radiographic findings. Few other diagnostic modalities provide useful data. Bone
scintigraphy with planar imaging is used in the clinical setting to detect implant
loosening; however, data are equivocal regarding the efficacy of this imaging modality.
Single photon emission CT may increase the sensitivity and specificity of boneSEND FEEDBACK

scintigraphy; however, it is not widely used in the diagnosis of aseptic loosening.16 Bone
scintigraphy may be positive more than 12 months postoperatively in 10% of
asymptomatic patients with a cemented or uncemented implant.17 In addition, markers
of bone turnover, such as urine telopeptides, do not provide enough information to
make a definitive diagnosis of implant loosening.
Flourine-18 2-flouro-2-deoxy-D-glucose PET may be performed to distinguish septic
loosening from aseptic loosening; however, this is not a highly sensitive or specific
imaging modality for this application.18 In addition, flourine-18 2-flouro-2-deoxy-D-
glucose PET is not definitively able to determine aseptic loosening. Positive flourine-18 2-
flouro-2-deoxy-D-glucose PET results with uptake only around the head and neck of the
prosthesis must be interpreted with a degree of suspicion.19
Management
Surgical indications for patients with radiographic lucency in the absence of clinical findings
are controversial. Indications depend on the size and extent of the lesion and the patient’s
functional demands and life expectancy.
Surgical treatment options range from débridement and bone grafting with component
retention to component exchange.
Surgical treatment generally is indicated in patients with an implant that is aseptically loose
because the natural history of this condition is progressive, with frequent implant and/or bone
fractures.
Treatment options rely on available bone stock.
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons and Paprosky classification systems
define the degree of bone loss and treatment options for the acetabular and femoral sides.
Acetabular treatment options range from component exchange to the use of acetabular
augments, cup-cage implants, antiprotrusio implants, and custom triflange implants for
severe bone loss.
Femoral treatment options range from component exchange to the use of fully porous-
coated monoblock or modular stems.
In revision femoral arthroplasty, noncemented fixation generally is indicated. Because of
loss of cancellous bone, interdigitation of polymethylmethacrylate cement is difficult in

primarily cortical bone.

Management
After identified, substantial radiolucency must be closely monitored via serial
radiographs and physical examinations. Revision arthroplasty frequently is
recommended for patients with aseptic loosening. The natural history of aseptic
loosening includes prosthetic and/or bony fracture; therefore, surgical management is
recommended.
In implants without frank evidence of loosening, surgical indications are more variable
and depend on the size and extent of the lesion and on the patient’s functional demands
and life expectancy. Surgical treatment options include lesion débridement and bone
grafting versus component exchange.
Treatment options for aseptic acetabular loosening primarily depend on the remaining
host bone stock. Numerous classification systems exist, including the American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons and Paprosky classifications, to define the degree of bone loss
and treatment options.20,21 If 50% of the acetabulum is supported with bony contact,
evidence suggests that the primary acetabular components can be used in revision
surgery.22 In patients with an unsupported acetabular rim or column loss, more
advanced implants, such as augments, cup-cage implants, or custom triflange
components, may be used.
The Paprosky and American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons classification systems
also are used to categorize the degree of femoral bone loss and subsequent treatment
options.23,24 In patients in whom sufficient metaphyseal bone exists, primary implants
may be used. In patients with an unsupportive metaphysis and supportive diaphysis,
long uncemented femoral stems are indicated, with monoblock or modular components.
In patients with an unsupportive diaphysis, salvage system options, such as allograft-
prosthetic composite or proximal femur replacement, are considered.
